problem: Earlier deep-RL navigation work was mostly trained and tested on the same distribution, often in synthetic or small indoor scenes. Earlier Street View instruction datasets were either small (e.g. 500 panoramas), used simplified action spaces where the agent always faces a traversable edge (Touchdown, Formulaic Maps), or had no disjoint train/test regions. Together these leave open whether agents can follow directions in large, visually noisy real-world environments and transfer to unseen areas and cities.
motivation: People with printed or GPS directions can readily navigate a city they have never visited, so language could bridge the generalisation gap that limits deep RL navigation. Google Street View combined with Google Maps driving directions allows a very large, realistic, geographically separated benchmark: 613k routes averaging about 125 steps. Transfer can then be tested within Manhattan, in a different city (Pittsburgh), and with more instructions than seen in training.
key_idea: The paper introduces StreetNav, a StreetLearn/Street View instruction-following RL suite with three difficulty tiers. RL agents (IMPALA-based) fuse CNN image features, LSTM text features and waypoint thumbnails, and a similarity-based hard-attention module picks which instruction to follow and when to switch.
insight: Factoring instruction selection out of the policy (hard attention over thumbnail-observation similarity) matters most when the task is hard or longer than in training. On the goal-only task Hard-A reaches 17.3% on NYC test vs 11.3% for the concatenation agent, and Hard-A_tuned degrades more gracefully with 6-8 instructions (Table 5). Concatenating all instructions wins only in the intermediate task and cannot generalise to more instructions. Four ablations are informative: (1) a No-Directions agent reaches 41.5% NYC test in the step-by-step task purely by exploiting the waypoint reward signal and one-way street traffic direction, so waypoint signalling leaks information; (2) language carries most of the value, since No-Thumb (66.1) far exceeds No-Text (47.1) on NYC test; (3) supervised student/teacher forcing fits training (95.0) but collapses on test (23.9 / 5.5) because agents never see the consequences of their errors; (4) end-to-end learned 2-layer CNN features beat ImageNet/Places ResNet features.
method: StreetNav environment: undirected graph of Street View panoramas; the agent sees a 60° 84x84 RGB crop and has 5 actions (forward along the best-aligned edge in its view cone, else NO-OP; rotate ±10°, ±30°); 1000-step limit; train in Lower Manhattan, validate in Midtown, test in a separate NYC area and in Pittsburgh.

Three task variants of increasing difficulty: Task 3 step-by-step (one instruction at a time, auto-switch at waypoints, waypoint rewards); Task 2 (full instruction list + waypoint rewards); Task 1 (full list, goal reward only). Training uses reward shaping with early fractional rewards within 50 m of waypoints/goal, never used at evaluation.

Multimodal encoder: word-level LSTM over GloVe embeddings for instructions; a shared 2-layer CNN for observations and start/end thumbnails; a 3-layer 256-unit MLP fuses (instruction, thumbnails), and a second MLP fuses that with the observation; the result feeds a policy LSTM that outputs π and V; previous action/reward are optional inputs.
Non-attentional IMPALA-derived agents: concatenate all instruction representations (All-Concat) or sum them (All-Sum) before fusion; the policy decides implicitly which instruction to use.

Hard attention (Hard-A): selects the instruction whose thumbnail is closest to the current observation, via argmax of softmax(-||t_i - x||_2), making the model sub-differentiable. Switching is triggered by the waypoint signal when available; otherwise (Task 1) by a similarity threshold τ tuned on validation, used only at evaluation.
Soft attention (Soft-A): stacked-attention-style weights h_i = W_a tanh(W_x x + W_t t_i) re-weight instructions and thumbnails.

Training: IMPALA asynchronous actor-critic, up to 1B steps, curriculum from Task 3 to Task 2 ('tuned'), stochastic MDP (forward fails with p=0.001) against memorisation; baselines include supervised student/teacher forcing on shortest-path actions.

setting.backbone: 2-layer CNN + word-level LSTM (GloVe) + fusion MLPs + policy LSTM, trained from scratch with IMPALA actor-critic RL
setting.training_data: StreetNav NYC train split: 580,415 routes in Lower Manhattan with Google Maps driving instructions and Street View thumbnails; up to 1 billion environment steps of RL per agent; curriculum from Task 3 to Task 2
setting.observation: monocular RGB (60° crop, 84x84) from Street View panorama + list of text instructions with start/end thumbnail images (+ previous action/reward, i.e. waypoint-reached signal, in Tasks 2/3)
setting.action_space: 5 discrete actions: move forward along graph edge (NO-OP if none in view cone), rotate ±10°, rotate ±30°
setting.privileged: none in Task 1 (goal-only). In Tasks 2/3 the environment's waypoint-reached reward signal is an agent input at test time, and in Task 3 the environment auto-switches to the next instruction.

numbers_note: Task names and several model names (All-Concat / All-Sum, No-Dir, etc.) were unexpanded LaTeX macros in the source, so method and task labels here are reconstructed; Hard-A, Soft-A and All-* appear literally. The only metric is 'percentage of goals reached' (SR), mean±std over 3 runs. Training-split numbers are omitted. Table 5 (larger instruction lists) reports only per-instruction-count SR, with no aggregate or std. The Pittsburgh test set and the NYC test area are both recorded as split 'test' and distinguished in 'extra'.
results: In the step-by-step task, Hard-A reaches 72.7% on NYC test and 46.6% on Pittsburgh. This beats all ablations and the supervised teacher-forcing baseline in the R2R style (23.9% / 8.6%), which fits training at 95.0% but does not generalise. With the full instruction list plus waypoint rewards, the concatenation agent is best (53.6% NYC / 33.5% Pittsburgh), but it cannot handle more instructions than seen in training. On the hardest goal-only task, Hard-A with threshold-based switching leads (17.3% NYC / 12.1% Pittsburgh vs 11.3% / 9.3% for concatenation), and all agents drop sharply when transferring to Pittsburgh.
limitations: Instructions are synthetic Google Maps driving directions, not natural human language.
Absolute performance on the realistic goal-only task stays low (~17% NYC, ~12% Pittsburgh), and transfer to a new city degrades markedly. RL also needs up to 1B environment steps per agent.

The waypoint-reward signal leaks exploitable information: an agent with no instructions reaches 41.5% via a one-way-street strategy. The switching threshold is hand-tuned rather than learned, and thumbnails are largely ignored by agents.

compares_to: No-Directions agents (with and without waypoint signal)
